ui.label: Fibonacci Recursive
ui.validation: Please enter a number between 1 and 6 (recursive tree grows fast)

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.content: Recursion solves a big problem by splitting it into **smaller problems of the same shape**. The Fibonacci definition F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2) is naturally recursive.
items: **Base Case**: F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1 are the [[primary|stopping conditions]]
Each call spawns **two** more calls, forming a recursion tree
Call state lives on the **call stack** until the Base Case returns
Results are then **combined** layer by layer into the final answer

sections.heading: Operation Complexity
sections.content: Because every call produces two sub-calls, the number of calls roughly doubles with each extra level.
items: **Time complexity**: [[danger|O(2ⁿ)]] — call count grows exponentially with n
**Space complexity**: [[warning|O(n)]] — the maximum call-stack depth is n
Naive recursion becomes noticeably slow once n reaches around 40

sections.heading: Why It Is So Slow
sections.content: The recursion tree shows identical subproblems (such as f(2)) being **recomputed** a huge number of times.
items: **Overlapping subproblems** are the root cause of the inefficiency
**Memoization**: cache computed results so each repeated subproblem is solved once, cutting time to [[success|O(n)]]; it uses the same recurrence as DP, just top-down
Better still, use **dynamic programming** to compute bottom-up and avoid recursion overhead entirely
